subject: Clarifying default capture: streaming tokens vs finalized outputs
messages:
From: Sam Reynolds <sam.reynolds@brightbank.com>
To: mateo_alvarez <mateo.alvarez@redwood.inference.com>
Date: Thu, 13 Aug 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Questions on default log capture and what is considered persistent

Hi Mateo,

Thanks for taking this — a couple of follow-ups from our security review:

1) When customers use streaming (token-by-token) responses, does Redwood persist the streamed buffer anywhere by default while the session is active, or is nothing written until the final output is produced?

2) How do you categorize: user prompt, model-generated suggestion, and reranked candidate? Which of those are treated as customer data, and which are considered derivative artifacts by default?

3) If a customer provides file attachments (e.g., PDFs) as part of a request, are those stored in the same retention window as text requests or treated differently?

4) We need a plain-language example workflow for deletion requests (our legal team likes flows with steps).

Appreciate anything concise you can share. If easier, we can take a short call — happy to loop in our cloud security folks.

Best,
Sam

Hi Sam — thanks for the clear list. High-level answers below; Kim will add the technical specifics and I'll attach a short matrix for clarity. If that looks good we can turn this into a one-page you can share with legal.

Summary (short):
- Streaming buffer: ephemeral by default — tokens buffered in-memory at the runtime and not written to persistent storage until a finalization event (completion or end-of-session) occurs.
- Prompt vs derivative: user-supplied prompts are treated as request data; model outputs and intermediate candidates are considered derived artifacts. By default both are retained under the standard capture horizon unless the customer opts out/configures a different policy.
- Attachments: files included in requests are stored as request artifacts and follow the same retention controls, but we surface them separately in audit logs and can apply stricter residency or deletion paths on request.
- Deletion workflow: we can provide a step-by-step runbook (see attached matrix).

Action items:
- Kim (cc) will provide TTLs, default retention windows, and residencies per deployment type (hosted vs EU private).
- I'll upload a short matrix and an example deletion flow (retention-matrix.pdf).

Matt — thanks, and Sam if you want me to redact anything for customer-facing docs let me know.

Cheers,
Mateo Alvarez

From: kimberly_park <kimberly.park@redwood.inference.com>

Date: Thu, 13 Aug 2026 12:30:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Questions on default log capture and what is considered persistent

Sam — hi, Kim from Security & Compliance here. Quick technical clarifications and concrete examples so your reviewers have measurable items.

1) Streaming buffer behavior (runtime):
- Default: token-by-token streaming lives only in the serving runtime memory. Unless the request triggers a finalization (e.g., completion, explicit save, or session snapshot), we do not persist the transient buffer to the telemetry store.
- Edge case: if a long-running session is interrupted and customer has enabled session persistence, an in-flight snapshot may be written to a short-lived store (TTL 6 hours) to allow resume. This is opt-in.

2) Classification (how we label and store):
- user_prompt (request): stored as a request record. Default hosted capture: 45 days retention for requests in standard plan (configurable).
- model_response (finalized output): stored under generated artifact classification; default capture window 90 days for generated artifacts used for quality monitoring (again configurable by plan and by customer).
- intermediate_candidates / reranks: considered transient derivatives — by default we keep them for 7 days for debugging and rerun traceability, then purge automatically unless flagged for inspection.

3) File attachments:
- Attachments submitted with a request are stored encrypted (at-rest) and classify as request-attached-artifacts. Default retention matches request record (45 days), but attachments can be put into a separate retention bucket on request (for example, 30 days) and/or pinned to a different residency. We can supply an export and proof-of-deletion for attachments.

4) Deletion / erasure flow (plain-language):
Step A — Request received: customer submits erase request (via portal or API), provide identifiers (request IDs, timestamps).
Step B — Verification: we validate the requestor's identity and scope.
Step C — Locate artifacts: system maps request IDs to storage buckets (requests, generated-artifacts, attachments, audit logs).
Step D — Orchestrated erase: for each bucket we trigger deletion APIs; ephemeral caches are invalidated instantly, persisted stores are scheduled for immediate delete, and tombstones are written to the audit ledger.
Step E — Evidence: we generate an erasure receipt + deletion logs and share a downloadable bundle (or HubSpot/Drive link). Typical SLA for hosted: 48 hours from verified request.

Notes & examples:
- Example A (chat session): prompts (45d), final transcript (90d), intermediate suggestions (7d). Erasure of request ID X removes the prompt & transcript and triggers artifact purges; logs noting the erasure are retained for compliance audit (immutable, signed, 2 years).
- Example B (single API with attached PDF): PDF treated as request-attached-artifact; deletion removes object from storage and returns an audit receipt.

Attachments included: audit-evidence-stub.zip (contains sample erasure receipt + runbook snippet).

If you want a shorter one-page summary for legal I'll prepare it.
